items.followUp: State five postulates of Dalton’s atomic theory.

rubric.why: Identifies that electrons occupy specific permitted orbits with definite energies.
rubric.description: Electrons revolve in permitted orbits or shells, each with a definite energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electron orbits are fixed/permitted and have definite energy.

rubric.why: States the stability of an electron in an allowed orbit and the rule for energy changes.
rubric.description: An electron does not emit or absorb energy while remaining in a permitted orbit; it absorbs or emits energy when it jumps between orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for no energy change in a permitted orbit and 1 mark for absorption/emission during a transition.

rubric.why: Includes Bohr’s quantisation rule and the relation between energy change and radiation.
rubric.description: Electron angular momentum is quantised (mvr = nh/2π); a transition involves a photon with energy equal to the difference between the two energy levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for quantised angular momentum and 1 mark for the photon/energy-difference rule.

modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in certain permitted circular paths called orbits or shells.
Each permitted orbit has a definite, fixed energy.
An electron does not emit or absorb energy while it remains in a permitted orbit.
An electron absorbs or emits energy when it jumps from one orbit to another; the energy change is ΔE = hν.
The angular momentum of an electron in an allowed orbit is quantised: mvr = nh/2π.

items.followUp: Describe the steps used to write the chemical formula of calcium nitrate.

rubric.why: Begins by identifying the symbols or formulae of the constituent ions/elements.
rubric.description: Write the symbols or formulae of the positive and negative ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for writing or identifying the constituent symbols/formulae.

rubric.why: Places the positive ion before the negative ion in the formula.
rubric.description: Write the positive ion first and the negative ion second.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct order.

rubric.why: Uses the valencies or charges to determine the subscripts.
rubric.description: Write the valencies and criss-cross them to become subscripts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for applying the criss-cross method correctly.

rubric.why: Ensures the final formula has the correct simplest subscripts and preserves polyatomic ions.
rubric.description: Reduce subscripts to the simplest whole-number ratio and use brackets around a polyatomic ion when needed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for simplification and correct bracket use where applicable.

modelAnswer: Write the symbols or formulae of the positive and negative ions, with the positive ion first.
Write the valency of each ion.
Criss-cross the valencies to become subscripts of the other ion.
Reduce the subscripts to the simplest whole-number ratio; use brackets around a polyatomic ion if its subscript is greater than one.
For example, Ca²⁺ and NO₃⁻ give Ca(NO₃)₂.

items.followUp: Define hydrogen bonding and explain its role in the properties of water.

rubric.why: Defines hydrogen bonding as a weak attractive force between suitable molecules or parts of molecules.
rubric.description: Hydrogen bonding is a weak attraction involving hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom and another electronegative atom.
rubric.how: Award marks for identifying it as an attraction/force and describing the required hydrogen–electronegative-atom arrangement.

rubric.why: Identifies the atoms commonly involved in hydrogen bonding.
rubric.description: Hydrogen is covalently bonded to F, O, or N, and is attracted to a lone pair on F, O, or N of a neighbouring molecule.
rubric.how: Award marks for naming the covalently bonded H–F/O/N pair and the neighbouring electronegative atom/lone pair.

rubric.why: Provides a correct example that explains hydrogen bonding between molecules.
rubric.description: In water, the partially positive hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to the partially negative oxygen of another molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly explaining hydrogen bonding between water molecules.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is a weak intermolecular attraction involving a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom and an electronegative atom of another molecule.
It occurs when hydrogen is bonded to fluorine, oxygen, or nitrogen and is attracted to a lone pair on F, O, or N in a neighbouring molecule.
In water, the partially positive hydrogen atom of one H₂O molecule is attracted to the partially negative oxygen atom of another H₂O molecule.
This attraction between neighbouring water molecules is a hydrogen bond.

items.followUp: Define evaporation and explain how temperature, surface area, and humidity affect its rate.

rubric.why: Defines evaporation as the escape of surface particles into vapour below the boiling point.
rubric.description: Evaporation is the change of a liquid into vapour from its surface, and can occur below its boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition including surface escape or the below-boiling-point feature.

rubric.why: States the effect of temperature on evaporation.
rubric.description: Higher temperature increases the rate of evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction and effect.

rubric.why: States the effect of exposed surface area on evaporation.
rubric.description: A larger exposed surface area increases the rate of evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction and effect.

rubric.why: Explains at least one further factor affecting evaporation correctly.
rubric.description: Higher humidity slows evaporation; greater wind speed or more volatile liquids increase it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing humidity, wind speed, or the nature of the liquid.

modelAnswer: Evaporation is the change of a liquid into vapour from its surface; it can occur at temperatures below the boiling point.
A higher temperature increases the rate of evaporation because more particles have enough energy to escape.
A larger exposed surface area increases the rate of evaporation.
Higher humidity decreases evaporation, while greater wind speed increases it; more volatile liquids evaporate faster.

items.followUp: Define an electrolyte and distinguish between strong and weak electrolytes with examples.

rubric.why: Defines an electrolyte by its ion formation and electrical conduction in the appropriate state.
rubric.description: An electrolyte produces mobile ions and conducts electricity when molten or in aqueous solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a definition linking ions to electrical conduction.

rubric.why: Explains the strong type in terms of the extent of ionisation and its conductivity.
rubric.description: A strong electrolyte ionises almost completely in solution and conducts electricity well; examples include HCl, NaOH, or NaCl.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for near-complete ionisation and 1 mark for a suitable example or its high conductivity.

rubric.why: Explains the weak type in terms of partial ionisation and its conductivity.
rubric.description: A weak electrolyte ionises only partially in solution and conducts electricity weakly; examples include acetic acid or ammonium hydroxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for partial ionisation and 1 mark for a suitable example or its weak conductivity.

modelAnswer: An electrolyte is a substance that produces mobile ions when molten or dissolved in water and therefore conducts electricity.
A strong electrolyte ionises almost completely in aqueous solution and conducts electricity well; examples include hydrochloric acid and sodium chloride.
A weak electrolyte ionises only partially in aqueous solution and conducts electricity weakly; examples include acetic acid and ammonium hydroxide.

items.followUp: Compare a true solution and a colloid using particle size, settling, and the Tyndall effect.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the particle sizes of suspensions and colloids.
rubric.description: Suspension particles are larger than colloidal particles; colloidal particle size is approximately 1–1000 nm.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct comparison of relative size or the colloid size range.

rubric.why: Compares whether particles settle on standing.
rubric.description: Suspension particles settle on standing, whereas colloidal particles remain dispersed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly contrasting settling behaviour.

rubric.why: Compares separation by ordinary filtration.
rubric.description: Suspension particles can be separated by ordinary filtration; colloidal particles pass through ordinary filter paper.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct filtration comparison.

rubric.why: Identifies the colloid’s light-scattering behaviour.
rubric.description: Colloids scatter light and show the Tyndall effect; suspensions also scatter light because their particles are large.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying light scattering/Tyndall effect in colloids.

modelAnswer: Suspension particles are larger than colloidal particles; colloidal particles are approximately 1–1000 nm in size.
Suspension particles settle on standing, whereas colloidal particles remain dispersed.
Suspension particles can be separated by ordinary filtration; colloidal particles pass through ordinary filter paper.
Colloids scatter light and show the Tyndall effect.

items.followUp: Name the four common states of matter and give one property of each.

rubric.why: Gives the defining features of matter.
rubric.description: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both mass and occupying space.

rubric.why: Names the three physical states requested.
rubric.description: The three physical states are solid, liquid, and gas.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for all three states.

modelAnswer: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space.
The three physical states of matter are solid, liquid, and gas.

items.followUp: Define a mixture and give one example.

rubric.why: Defines a compound as a chemically combined pure substance with a fixed composition.
rubric.description: A compound is a pure substance formed when two or more elements are chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for chemical combination and fixed proportion/composition.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example and, where applicable, its formula.
rubric.description: A correct example is water (H₂O), sodium chloride (NaCl), or carbon dioxide (CO₂).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct compound example.

modelAnswer: A compound is a pure substance formed when two or more elements are chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
Water (H₂O) is an example of a compound.
